lines.text: everything merely given and actual, is corrupted by the
curse of the inadequate, unfulfilled and transitory. It is just
this which we feel and dimly suspect when we speak of our
real self and its fulfilment. But have we the will to carry
through this feeling? Are we really ready, when the beyond,
when God confronts us, to surrender the world? Hence are
we truly ready, when God confronts us in the figure of Jesus,
to become His disciples and to allow the world to be simply
the world? This is the choice which is in question here. This
is the point on which we are called to make a clear-sighted
decision, namely that what at times we probably dimly
surmise, what at times we no doubt long for—that it should
really become the controlling force in our lives. Here is the
decisive issue which Jesus puts before men. The light which
He sheds is the light of the eternal world; the joy which He
bestows is supernatural joy. Truly to desire this light and
this joy, hence to be His disciple, means to live as though one
no longer really belonged to this world. Do we desire this
with all our hearts?
That restless unappeasable surmise that our true self
cannot find its fulfilment in this world, in this-worldly values
and aims, gifts and duties, usually comes over us only when
we disastrously fail in our desires and strivings, when that
to which we had lost our hearts, that which made our little
world dear and familiar and homely to us, is shattered. Or
again it visits us when a sinister future looms threateningly
before us, for which we feel we are no match, and in whose
sombre shadows the colours of the present fade. At such
moments as these when the world in which we live suddenly
strikes us as alien, when in the midst of its homelessness we
long for our true home, we are visited by this intimation of
the beyond. Then it may well be that we feel as if the affairs
of this world in which we are so deeply implicated were a
confusing dream from which we must awake. The actualities
in which we live seem to us unreal and ghostly. "There are
dark moments of dismay and moods of sad heart-sickness,
when all hovers dim and ghostly, in a sea of mist."1 But
